title: Writing Kernel with AI
text:
Welcome to Kernel Engineering
Accelerated computing and modern artificial intelligence rest on a single engineering discipline: extracting peak theoretical throughput from hardware.
Whether training frontier foundation models or serving millions of concurrent inference tokens, the software stack converges onto specialized computational kernels. Writing fast kernels is not a matter of guesswork or trial-and-error—it is an empirical science governed by the physics of computation: arithmetic intensity, memory bandwidth, latency hiding, and hardware execution hierarchies.

The Trajectory of This Book
This curriculum spans six rigorous parts designed to take you from first principles to the cutting edge:

Part I: Parallelism, from the CPU up: Understand how modern CPUs achieve massive throughput via SIMD vectorization and multi-threading before stepping into the GPU execution hierarchy: warps, streaming multiprocessors, memory coalescing, and the Roofline model.
Part II: The GEMM Worklog: Naive → cuBLAS: Master General Matrix Multiply (GEMM)—the operation that comprises over 90% of deep learning FLOPs. Step by step, elevate a naive kernel achieving 1.3% of GPU capacity to a hierarchical warp-tiled and Tensor Core (WMMA) implementation rivaling NVIDIA’s cuBLAS library.
Part III: Attention & Profiling: Diagnose hardware bottlenecks using NVIDIA Nsight Compute like a compiler engineer. Construct FlashAttention v1 from scratch, utilizing the online softmax algorithm to eliminate high-bandwidth memory bottlenecks.
Part IV: The Modern Frontier: Explore modern production kernels running on Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) architectures: FlashAttention-2/3/4, TMA asynchronous copy, WGMMA, Triton, CUTLASS, CuTe-DSL, PagedAttention, and NVFP4.
Part V: AI-Written Kernels: Analyze DeepSeek’s ultra-compact, high-performance kernels (FlashMLA and DeepGEMM). Step into the future of kernel development: using autonomous LLM agents (e.g., DeepMind AlphaEvolve, KernelBench) with profiler-in-the-loop guidance.
Part VI: Kernel Engineering Capstone Projects: Put your skills into practice with industry-grade capstone specifications developed with Crusoe, complete with verification harnesses, performance benchmarks, and demo-day technical presentations.

title: Parallelism on the CPU
text:
Parallelism on the CPU
Before programming thousands of lockstep cores on a GPU, we must build a mechanical understanding of how modern CPUs execute concurrent and parallel work. High-performance computing is fundamentally an exercise in orchestrating physical execution units while feeding them data fast enough to prevent pipeline stalls.
Modern CPUs extract performance across three distinct tiers of parallelism: 1. Instruction-Level Parallelism (ILP): Pipelining, superscalar dispatch, out-of-order execution, and branch prediction within a single core. 2. Data-Level Parallelism (SIMD): Single Instruction, Multiple Data execution where one machine instruction operates over a register packed with multiple independent values. 3. Thread-Level Parallelism (TLP): Multiple independent execution streams running concurrently across physical and logical processor cores.

title: Parallelism on the CPU
text:
1. Instruction-Level Parallelism (ILP) and Microarchitecture
A modern CPU core is not a simple sequential state machine. It is an asynchronous processing pipeline designed to retire multiple micro-operations (uops) per clock cycle.
       +--------------------------------------------------------+
       |                  Fetch & Branch Predict                |
       +---------------------------+----------------------------+
                                   |
       +---------------------------v----------------------------+
       |                  Decode & Macro-Op Fusion              |
       +---------------------------+----------------------------+
                                   |
       +---------------------------v----------------------------+
       |          Register Alias Table (RAT) & Rename           |
       +---------------------------+----------------------------+
                                   |
       +---------------------------v----------------------------+
       |            Reorder Buffer (ROB) & Reservation          |
       +-------+------------+------------+------------+---------+
               |            |            |            |
          +----v----+  +----v----+  +----v----+  +----v----+
          | ALU Port|  | ALU Port|  | SIMD/FMA|  |Load/Store|
          +---------+  +---------+  +---------+  +---------+

The Out-of-Order Engine

Instruction Fetch & Branch Prediction: The CPU fetches instructions ahead of the current program counter using branch target buffers (BTB) and direction predictors. When a branch is mispredicted, the entire speculative pipeline must be flushed, costing 15 to 20 cycles of wasted energy.
Decode and Micro-op Generation: Complex x86 instructions are broken down into simpler, RISC-like micro-operations (uops).
Register Renaming & Reservation Stations: To break false register dependencies (Write-After-Read and Write-After-Write hazards), the CPU maps architectural registers (e.g., rax, ymm0) to a much larger pool of physical registers.
Out-of-Order (OoO) Dispatch: Independent instructions whose operands are ready in the cache or register file execute out of program order across parallel execution ports.
In-Order Retirement: The Reorder Buffer (ROB) ensures that memory state updates and architectural register commits happen in strict program order, guaranteeing consistent exception semantics.

text:
3. Thread-Level Parallelism: Heavyweight vs Lightweight
To leverage multi-core CPUs, applications distribute work across threads. How threads are modeled dramatically impacts context switching overhead and memory footprint.
OS Heavyweight Threads:
  [Kernel Scheduler] ---> [Core 0: OS Thread (2-8 MB Stack)]  (Switch: ~1-3 us)
                     ---> [Core 1: OS Thread (2-8 MB Stack)]

Lightweight User-Space Green Threads / Fibers:
  [OS Thread / SM]    ---> [Fiber A (2 KB)] -> [Fiber B (2 KB)] -> [Fiber C (2 KB)]

The Cost of OS Threads
POSIX threads (pthread_create) or OpenMP workers (#pragma omp parallel for) allocate their own kernel task structure and a fixed memory stack (typically 2 MB to 8 MB). - When an OS thread context switches, the CPU must switch privilege rings into the kernel, save and restore architectural register state (including wide AVX-512 state), and suffer TLB and cache pollution. - Total latency: 1,000 to 3,000 CPU cycles (1–3 microseconds).


User-Space Concurrency (M:N Models)
Modern programming environments decouple logical concurrency from physical OS threads: - Go Goroutines: Allocate a dynamic 2 KB stack that grows on demand. The runtime multiplexes thousands of goroutines across a fixed thread pool (GOMAXPROCS), switching in user space within ~10 to 50 nanoseconds. - Java Virtual Threads (Project Loom): Suspendable continuation objects stored on the garbage-collected heap. - Rust Tokio: Futures compiled into zero-allocation state machines driven by a lock-free work-stealing executor.

title: Roofline Lab: Predict Then Measure
text:
Roofline Lab: Predict Then Measure
Every high-performance kernel is bounded by one of two physical constraints: 1. Compute Bound: The execution units (ALUs, FPUs, Tensor Cores) are saturated executing instructions; the memory interface has idle bandwidth. 2. Memory Bound: The execution units starve waiting for data to arrive from off-chip DRAM (HBM or GDDR); arithmetic throughput is a fraction of hardware peak.
Before writing a single line of CUDA, a kernel engineer must predict which regime the workload inhabits. Writing faster assembly or unrolling loops inside a memory-bound kernel achieves zero speedup. Conversely, optimizing memory tiling for a kernel already compute-bound yields diminishing returns.

title: Roofline Lab: Predict Then Measure
text:
1. The Roofline Model Formulation
The Roofline Model, formulated by Williams et al. (Berkeley), visualizes maximum achievable performance as a function of Operational Intensity (also called Arithmetic Intensity).

Definitions
\[\text{Operational Intensity } (I) = \frac{\text{Total Arithmetic Operations (FLOPs)}}{\text{Total Bytes Transferred from DRAM (Bytes)}}\]
\[\text{Attainable Performance } (P) = \min\left(\text{Peak Hardware Compute } (P_{\text{peak}}), \text{Peak Memory Bandwidth } (B) \times I\right)\]
Performance (TFLOP/s)
  ^
  |                           Peak Hardware Compute (P_peak)
  |                       +--------------------------------------- (Compute Bound)
  |                      /
  |                     /
  |                    /  Memory Bandwidth Slope
  |                   /   (P = Bandwidth * I)
  |                  /
  |                 /
  |                /      (Memory Bound)
  |               /
  +--------------+------------------------------------------------>
  0             I* (Ridge Point)         Operational Intensity (FLOPs/Byte)


The Ridge Point (\(I^*\))
The intersection between the memory bandwidth slope and the peak compute roof defines the Ridge Point (\(I^*\)):
\[I^* = \frac{P_{\text{peak}}}{B_{\text{peak}}}\]

If a workload’s intensity \(I < I^*\): The workload is strictly memory-bound. Maximum possible throughput is capped at \(B_{\text{peak}} \times I\). To go faster, you must reduce memory traffic (e.g. through kernel fusion or caching).
If a workload’s intensity \(I \ge I^*\): The workload is compute-bound. Maximum possible throughput is capped at \(P_{\text{peak}}\). To go faster, you must optimize instruction throughput, eliminate warp divergence, or switch to lower-precision numeric formats (e.g. FP16, BF16, FP8).

title: Roofline Lab: Predict Then Measure
text:
3. Dissecting Common Machine Learning Operations
Let us calculate the operational intensity for four fundamental deep learning operations executed on an NVIDIA A100 (SXM4: \(B = 2,039 \text{ GB/s}\), \(P_{\text{vector}} = 19.5 \text{ TFLOP/s}\)).

Case 1: Vector Addition (\(y = x + z\))
Given two vectors of length \(N = 10^7\) FP32 elements: - Operations: \(N\) additions = \(10^7\) FLOPs. - Memory Traffic: - Read \(x\): \(10^7 \times 4 \text{ B} = 40 \text{ MB}\). - Read \(z\): \(10^7 \times 4 \text{ B} = 40 \text{ MB}\). - Write \(y\): \(10^7 \times 4 \text{ B} = 40 \text{ MB}\). - Total Memory = \(120 \text{ MB} = 1.2 \times 10^8 \text{ Bytes}\). - Operational Intensity: \[I = \frac{10^7 \text{ FLOPs}}{1.2 \times 10^8 \text{ Bytes}} \approx 0.0833 \text{ FLOPs/Byte}\] - Analysis: \(I = 0.0833 \ll I^* = 9.6\). Strictly memory bound. - Maximum Theoretical Throughput: \[\text{Throughput} = 2,039 \text{ GB/s} \times 0.0833 \text{ FLOPs/Byte} \approx 169.8 \text{ GFLOP/s}\] The GPU achieves less than 0.9% of its FP32 compute capability. The ALU cores spend 99% of their time stalled waiting for memory controllers.


Case 2: LayerNorm / RMSNorm
RMSNorm computes: \(y_i = \frac{x_i}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2 + \epsilon}} \cdot \gamma_i\). For a hidden dimension \(d = 4096\): - Operations per token: - Square: \(d\) FLOPs. - Sum reduction: \(d - 1\) FLOPs. - Mean, add \(\epsilon\), reciprocal square root (rsqrt): \(\sim 4\) FLOPs. - Scale by \(\gamma\) and write: \(2d\) FLOPs. - Total \(\approx 4d \approx 16,384\) FLOPs. - Memory per token (unfused naive PyTorch): - Read input \(x\): \(d \times 4 \text{ B} = 16 \text{ KB}\). - Intermediates written and re-read from global memory: \(\sim 3 \times 16 \text{ KB} = 48 \text{ KB}\). - Write output \(y\): \(16 \text{ KB}\). - Total \(\sim 80 \text{ KB}\). - Operational Intensity: \[I = \frac{16,384 \text{ FLOPs}}{81,920 \text{ Bytes}} \approx 0.20 \text{ FLOPs/Byte}\] - Analysis: Completely memory bound. This is why fused normalization kernels (which keep intermediates in registers and shared memory) deliver massive 5x to 10x speedups.


Case 3: Dense Matrix Multiplication (GEMM)
Compute \(C = A \times B\) where \(A, B, C \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}\), with \(M = K = N = 4096\): - Operations: \(2 \times M \times N \times K = 2 \times 4096^3 \approx 137.4 \times 10^9 \text{ FLOPs}\) (137.4 GFLOPs). - Minimum Algorithmic Memory (I/O): - Read \(A\): \(4096^2 \times 4 \text{ B} = 67.1 \text{ MB}\). - Read \(B\): \(4096^2 \times 4 \text{ B} = 67.1 \text{ MB}\). - Write \(C\): \(4096^2 \times 4 \text{ B} = 67.1 \text{ MB}\). - Total \(\approx 201.3 \text{ MB}\). - Operational Intensity (with perfect reuse): \[I_{\text{optimal}} = \frac{1.374 \times 10^{11} \text{ FLOPs}}{2.013 \times 10^8 \text{ Bytes}} \approx 682.6 \text{ FLOPs/Byte}\] - Analysis: \(I = 682.6 > I^* = 9.6\) (and even \(> I^*_{\text{Tensor}} = 153.0\)). Dense GEMM is thoroughly compute-bound when memory reuse is leveraged via shared memory tiling!

text:
4. The Multi-Tier Roofline (Hierarchy of Limits)
Modern GPUs have multiple memory tiers. A kernel that exhausts L2 cache bandwidth or shared memory bandwidth hits an intermediate roofline before reaching DRAM:
Throughput (TFLOP/s)
  ^
  |                                      Tensor Core Peak (989 TFLOP/s)
  |                       +--------------------------------------------
  |                      / (SM SRAM Bandwidth: ~19 TB/s)
  |                     /
  |                    /  (L2 Cache Bandwidth: ~5.2 TB/s)
  |                   /
  |                  /   (HBM3 DRAM Bandwidth: ~3.35 TB/s)
  |                 /
  +----------------+--------------------------------------------------->
  0                                        Operational Intensity (FLOPs/B)

HBM / DRAM Bandwidth: The slowest and largest layer. Optimization goal: load each byte from DRAM exactly once into on-chip memory.
L2 Cache Bandwidth: Over 2x to 3x faster than DRAM. Shared across all SMs.
Shared Memory / L1 SRAM Bandwidth: Over 5x to 8x faster than DRAM (~19 TB/s aggregate on H100). Serves warps inside a single SM.
Register File Bandwidth: Over 30 TB/s aggregate bandwidth. The only memory tier that can feed execution units at full single-cycle latency.

By comparing these two percentages, you instantly know whether to optimize memory access patterns or computational instructions.

title: The CUDA Programming Model & GPU Puzzles
text:
The CUDA Programming Model & GPU Puzzles
Modern GPUs execute programs using the SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) execution model. While SIMD on a CPU executes a single vector instruction over vector registers on a single core, SIMT executes hundreds of independent scalar threads grouped into lockstep units called warps.
Writing effective CUDA kernels requires understanding both the logical programming abstractions and how the hardware scheduler physically maps them onto silicon.

title: The CUDA Programming Model & GPU Puzzles
text:
1. The Logical vs Physical Hierarchy
CUDA defines a hierarchical programming model that scales seamlessly from a single-SM embedded chip (e.g. Jetson) to a massive data-center accelerator with 144 SMs (e.g. Hopper H100).
Logical Abstraction                     Physical Hardware
-------------------                     -----------------
Grid (Entire Kernel Launch)   ------>   GPU Device
  |
  +--> Thread Block (Cooperative) --->   Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)
         |
         +--> Warp (32 Threads)  ----->   Warp Scheduler & Execution Units
                |
                +--> Thread     ----->   CUDA Core / Register Slice

The Dimensions

Thread: The finest unit of execution. Each thread has its own program counter, private registers, and local memory stack.
Warp: A contiguous group of 32 threads. The warp is the fundamental unit of scheduling on the GPU. All 32 threads in a warp execute the same instruction simultaneously.
Thread Block (CTA - Cooperative Thread Array): A group of up to 1,024 threads. Threads within the same block reside on the same physical SM, share fast on-chip Shared Memory (SRAM), and can synchronize using barrier primitives (__syncthreads()).
Grid: The full set of thread blocks dispatched to execute a kernel. Thread blocks within a grid execute independently; there is no guaranteed execution order across blocks.

title: The CUDA Programming Model & GPU Puzzles
The CUDA Programming Model & GPU Puzzles
section: 3. Warp Divergence and the SIMT Execution Mask
text:
3. Warp Divergence and the SIMT Execution Mask
All 32 threads in a warp share a single instruction unit. If threads within a warp take different execution paths at a conditional branch (if / else), the hardware executes every branch path sequentially, disabling threads that are not on that path via a hardware execution mask.
Instruction Stream:
Thread 0-15:   Takes IF branch (condition is true)
Thread 16-31:  Takes ELSE branch (condition is false)

Execution Timeline:
Cycle 1-10:  [Thread 0-15 Active] [Thread 16-31 MASKED OFF] -> Executes IF body
Cycle 11-20: [Thread 0-15 MASKED OFF] [Thread 16-31 Active] -> Executes ELSE body
Reconverge:  [All Threads 0-31 Active]

The Cost of Divergence

When a warp diverges 2-ways, execution time roughly doubles.
When 32 threads take 32 distinct branch paths (e.g. switch(threadIdx.x % 32)), the warp serializes into 32 separate execution passes, dropping warp computational throughput to 3.1% of peak.



Best Practices to Eliminate Divergence

Align branches by warp boundary: Branches that depend strictly on blockIdx or threadIdx.x / 32 cause zero divergence because all 32 threads in the warp evaluate to the exact same condition.
Predicated Instructions: For tiny branches (1-2 instructions), the compiler automatically uses predicated instructions instead of jumping.
Use Intrinsic Math Primitives: Replace if (a < b) val = a; else val = b; with fminf(a, b), which compiles to a single non-branching instruction.

The Memory Hierarchy in Anger: Matrix Transpose
Writing fast GPU kernels is fundamentally about choreographing data movement through the memory hierarchy. While modern GPUs boast tens of teraflops of arithmetic power, every floating-point operation is useless if data cannot reach the functional units.
In this chapter, we dissect the GPU memory hierarchy, master global memory coalescing, resolve shared memory bank conflicts, and walk through the canonical optimization benchmark: Matrix Transpose.

title: The Memory Hierarchy in Anger: Matrix Transpose
text:
2. Global Memory Coalescing: The 10x Lever
When threads in a warp issue a read or write instruction to global memory, the memory controller does not process 32 separate individual 4-byte requests. Instead, it aggregates adjacent addresses into coalesced 32-byte or 128-byte memory transactions.

The Golden Rule of Coalescing

Consecutive threads in a warp (threadIdx.x from 0 to 31) must access consecutive memory addresses (address + 0, address + 4, …, address + 124).

Coalesced Access (Consecutive):
Threads:      T0   T1   T2   T3   ...  T31
               |    |    |    |         |
Memory Addr: 0x00 0x04 0x08 0x0C  ...  0x7C
Result: ONE single 128-byte transaction! (100% bus utilization)

Uncoalesced Strided Access (Column-wise):
Threads:      T0         T1         T2   ...  T31
               |          |          |         |
Memory Addr: 0x0000     0x1000     0x2000 ... 0x1F000 (Stride = N elements)
Result: 32 SEPARATE 32-byte transactions! (3.1% bus utilization!)
In the uncoalesced case, the GPU fetches \(32 \times 32 \text{ Bytes} = 1024 \text{ Bytes}\) over the physical memory bus to retrieve only \(32 \times 4 \text{ Bytes} = 128 \text{ Bytes}\) of useful data. 90% of your memory bandwidth is wasted.

title: The Memory Hierarchy in Anger: Matrix Transpose
text:
3. Shared Memory Bank Conflicts
Shared memory is organized into 32 independent memory banks, each with a word width of 4 bytes (32 bits).
Successive 32-bit words are assigned to successive banks in round-robin fashion: - bank_index = (byte_address / 4) % 32
Bank 0:  Word 0,  Word 32, Word 64 ...
Bank 1:  Word 1,  Word 33, Word 65 ...
...
Bank 31: Word 31, Word 63, Word 95 ...

The Conflict Condition

Conflict-Free: All 32 threads in a warp access different banks (or all threads broadcast-read the exact same word). The memory request completes in 1 cycle.
N-Way Bank Conflict: If \(N\) threads in a warp request different addresses that map to the same bank, the hardware must serialize the requests into \(N\) successive single-bank accesses. An 8-way conflict reduces shared memory throughput by \(8\times\).

title: GEMM Worklog I: Naive to Tiled
text:
GEMM Worklog I: Naive to Tiled
General Matrix Multiply (GEMM) is the computational engine of modern artificial intelligence. Fully connected layers, multi-head attention projections, convolutional layers (via im2col), and mixture-of-experts routers all compile down to GEMM:
\[C = \alpha (A \times B) + \beta C\]
where \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times K}\), \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times N}\), and \(C \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}\).
In this worklog, we embark on the canonical kernel engineering journey: elevating a naive GEMM achieving less than 1.5% of GPU capacity to a shared-memory tiled kernel achieving over 36% of theoretical peak compute.

title: GEMM Worklog I: Naive to Tiled
section: 2. The Breakthrough: Shared Memory 2D Block Tiling
text:
2. The Breakthrough: Shared Memory 2D Block Tiling
To escape the memory bottleneck, we must reuse loaded data.
Notice: - All threads in the same row \(i\) need the exact same value \(A_{i,k}\). - All threads in the same column \(j\) need the exact same value \(B_{k,j}\).
Instead of streaming from global memory for every multiply-add, thread blocks load a 2D tile of \(A\) and a 2D tile of \(B\) into ultra-fast on-chip Shared Memory (SRAM), synchronize, and then perform multiple arithmetic operations from SRAM.
               Global Memory (Slow HBM)
                     |
           (Coalesced Block Load)
                     v
             Shared Memory Tile
         s_a [TILE x TILE]   s_b [TILE x TILE]
                     |
       (All threads reuse data TILE times!)
                     v
             Registers & ALUs

Tile Dimensions and Reuse Factor
With a tile size of \(\text{TILE} = 32\): - Each thread loads 1 element of \(A\) and 1 element of \(B\) into shared memory. - During the inner multiplication loop, each loaded element is read and reused by 32 separate threads! - Global memory traffic drops by a factor of \(32\times\). - Operational intensity jumps from \(0.25 \text{ FLOPs/Byte}\) to: \[I_{\text{tiled}} = 0.25 \times 32 = \mathbf{8.0 \text{ FLOPs/Byte}}\]
At \(8.0 \text{ FLOPs/Byte}\), we are right next to the hardware Ridge Point (\(I^* = 9.6\)).

title: GEMM Worklog II: Registers & Warp Tiling
text:
GEMM Worklog II: Registers & Warp Tiling
While shared memory tiling dramatically cuts DRAM traffic, shared memory bandwidth itself becomes the bottleneck at high utilization. Reaching near-cuBLAS performance requires register tiling and vectorized memory instructions.

Micro-Tiling in Registers
Registers provide ~20 TB/s aggregate bandwidth. Instead of each thread calculating a single output element \(C_{i,j}\), each thread computes a \(TM imes TN\) block of elements (e.g. \(8 imes 8 = 64\) values per thread).


Vectorized Memory Loads with float4
Global and shared memory loads should be widened using 128-bit vector loads (float4 / int4):
// Load 4 consecutive floats in a single 128-bit transaction
float4 a_val = *reinterpret_cast<const float4*>(&A[idx]);


The Warptiling Hierarchy
Modern production kernels decompose matrix multiply into four distinct structural layers: 1. Grid Tile: Handled by the entire GPU grid across all SMs. 2. Block Tile: Handled by a single thread block using shared memory. 3. Warp Tile: Handled by a 32-thread warp executing synchronized sub-tiles. 4. Thread Tile: Handled by individual thread registers.
By structuring the kernel into a \(128 imes 128\) block tile and \(64 imes 64\) warp tiles with double buffering, manual register allocation reaches 93.7% of cuBLAS speed on NVIDIA Ampere hardware.

Profiling & Debugging Like a Pro
Optimization without profiling is speculation. Top kernel engineers diagnose bottlenecks systematically using the NVIDIA toolchain:

The Professional Diagnostic Stack

Debugging Sabotaged Kernels: 3 Classic Incident Scenarios

Incident 1: Silent Race Condition in Shared Memory: Threads write to s_data[threadIdx.x] and read from s_data[threadIdx.x + 1] without an intervening __syncthreads(). Detection: compute-sanitizer --tool racecheck ./my_kernel
Incident 2: Shared Memory Bank Conflicts: All 32 threads in a warp access different rows in the same shared memory bank simultaneously. Detection: NCU metric l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu_mem_shared.sum. Resolution: Stride padding (__shared__ float smem[32][33]).
Incident 3: Catastrophic Register Spilling: Kernel uses 80 registers per thread when the hardware limit per thread at target occupancy is 64. Excessive variables spill to local DRAM memory, increasing latency 100x. Detection: Compiler flag --ptxas-options=-v reporting spill stores / spill loads. Resolution: Kernel launch bound annotation __launch_bounds__(256, 2).

title: Attention: The Kernel That Ate the World & FlashAttention v1
text:
Attention: The Kernel That Ate the World & FlashAttention v1
Standard Transformer Attention computes:
\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{Softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V\]
For a sequence length \(N\) and head dimension \(d\) (\(N \gg d\)): - \(S = Q K^T\) generates an \(N \times N\) attention score matrix. - Traditional PyTorch implementations materialize \(S\) and \(P = \text{Softmax}(S)\) in global HBM memory (\(O(N^2)\) memory reads and writes). - For long contexts (\(N = 32k\) or \(128k\)), intermediate matrices consume gigabytes of memory and choke HBM bandwidth.

The Breakthrough: Online Softmax & Tiling
Tri Dao et al. introduced FlashAttention: compute the exact attention output without ever writing the \(N \times N\) intermediate attention matrix to global memory.
Traditional Attention (Memory-Bound):
  Q, K -> [Global HBM Write: S] -> [Global HBM Read: S] -> Softmax -> [Global HBM Write: P] -> [Global HBM Read: P] -> V -> Output
FlashAttention (Fused into SRAM):
  Load Blocks of Q, K, V into On-chip SRAM -> Compute Local Gemm -> Online Softmax Update -> Accumulate Output -> Single Global Write


The Online Softmax Formula
Traditional softmax requires two passes over the sequence: pass 1 to find the maximum \(m = \max(x_i)\), and pass 2 to compute \(\sum e^{x_i - m}\). Online softmax updates the running maximum \(m\) and normalization sum \(l\) incrementally as blocks stream through shared memory:
\[m_{\text{new}} = \max(m_{\text{prev}}, m_{\text{block}})\]
\[l_{\text{new}} = e^{m_{\text{prev}} - m_{\text{new}}} l_{\text{prev}} + e^{m_{\text{block}} - m_{\text{new}}} l_{\text{block}}\]
\[O_{\text{new}} = e^{m_{\text{prev}} - m_{\text{new}}} O_{\text{prev}} + P_{\text{block}} V_{\text{block}}\]

title: Beating cuBLAS on an H100
text:
Beating cuBLAS on an H100
NVIDIA’s Hopper H100 microarchitecture introduced two revolutionary hardware subsystems:

1. Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA)
In pre-Hopper architectures, threads in a warp explicitly load data from global memory into registers, then write from registers into shared memory. TMA executes multidimensional tensor transfers (e.g. 2D/3D tiles) directly between global HBM and shared memory asynchronously in hardware, completely bypassing the register file and consuming zero SM ALU cycles.


2. Warp Specialization
Instead of every thread in a block performing both memory loading and arithmetic: - Producer Warps (1-2 warps): Issue asynchronous TMA copy instructions to fetch upcoming tiles into double-buffered shared memory. - Consumer Warps (Warp Groups): Execute continuous WGMMA matrix multiply instructions without ever pausing for memory latency. - Hardware barrier arrive/wait primitives (cuda::barrier) synchronize producers and consumers with cycle-level precision.

title: Triton → CUTLASS → CuTe-DSL
text:
Triton → CUTLASS → CuTe-DSL
Kernel engineering in 2025-2026 has transitioned from hand-written CUDA C++ toward declarative and high-level DSL frameworks.

OpenAI Triton
Triton allows writing high-performance GPU kernels in idiomatic Python. The programmer writes code at the granularity of block tiles rather than individual threads. The Triton compiler handles intra-block scheduling, memory coalescing, and shared memory allocation automatically.
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, output_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE
    offsets = block_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_elements
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    tl.store(output_ptr + offsets, x + y, mask=mask)


CUTLASS & CuTe
NVIDIA CUTLASS 3.x is structured around CuTe: a C++ template library that unifies data layouts, coordinates, and hierarchical tensor tiling through mathematical layout algebra: \[  ext{Layout} = ( ext{Shape},     ext{Stride})\]

title: Inference-Serving Kernels
text:
Inference-Serving Kernels
LLM inference splits into two distinct execution regimes with radically different performance characteristics: 1. Prefill Phase: The prompt is processed in parallel. High operational intensity, strictly compute-bound. 2. Decode Phase: Tokens are generated autoregressively one by one. The model loads billions of weights to compute a single new vector. Strictly memory-bound!

PagedAttention (vLLM)
In standard inference, KV caches must be allocated as contiguous memory buffers. This leads to 60-80% memory waste due to internal and external memory fragmentation. PagedAttention treats KV cache memory like virtual memory pages in an operating system: - KV vectors are stored in non-contiguous 16-token page blocks. - A page table maps logical token positions to physical GPU memory addresses. - Result: Memory waste drops to near 0%, enabling 2-4x higher serving concurrency on the same hardware.

title: Blackwell & NVFP4

Blackwell & NVFP4
NVIDIA’s Blackwell (B200 / GB200) microarchitecture represents the state of the art in frontier hardware (2025-2026).

Blackwell Architectural Highlights

tcgen05 Tensor Cores: 5th generation Tensor Cores delivering 4x higher FP4 training and inference density compared to Hopper FP8.
Tensor Memory (TMEM): A dedicated ultra-fast on-chip memory structure decoupled from shared memory, specifically optimized for multi-tensor staging and GEMM accumulation.
NVFP4 Microscopic Scaling: 4-bit floating point format with micro-block scaling factors that preserves accuracy across large foundation models while doubling token throughput.

title: Flash Attention 4
text:
Flash Attention 4

The 2026 Frontier: Breaking the 1 PFLOPS Single-GPU Barrier
On Blackwell hardware, Tensor Core matrix multiply units run so extraordinarily fast that the normalization step in Softmax—historically a minor fraction of runtime—becomes the dominant bottleneck.
FlashAttention-4 introduces Adaptive Softmax: - Dynamically checks divergence between running block maximums and candidate maximums. - Skips full re-normalization when numerical differences fall below precision thresholds. - Overlaps Softmax correction entirely behind asynchronous WGMMA execution pipelines. - Written using modern Python CuTe-DSL, FA4 is the first kernel to achieve over 1 PFLOPS of sustained attention compute on a single processor.

title: PagedAttention and the KV Cache
text:
PagedAttention and the KV Cache
Autoregressive LLM serving is memory-bound in decode and capacity-bound in concurrency: each active sequence carries a growing key/value (KV) cache. Contiguous per-sequence KV allocations waste large fractions of GPU DRAM to fragmentation and over-reservation. PagedAttention (vLLM) borrows the OS virtual-memory idea—fixed-size blocks, a block table, allocate-on-demand—so attention kernels read logically contiguous tokens from physically non-contiguous KV blocks.
This chapter goes deeper than a one-paragraph mention in inference-serving notes: why contiguous KV fails, how block tables work, prefill vs decode implications, layout choices for custom kernels, and how to verify/benchmark paging behavior.

title: PagedAttention and the KV Cache
text:
Why contiguous KV wastes memory
For a sequence with maximum length \(L_{\max}\) and current length \(t\):

Reservation waste: many systems allocate KV for \(L_{\max}\) up front even while \(t \ll L_{\max}\).

External fragmentation: variable-length contiguous regions cannot pack tightly as sequences finish at different times.

Batching rigidity: contiguous layouts make sharing prefixes or compacting live sequences expensive.

Empirical reports in the PagedAttention / vLLM line of work put waste often in the 60–80% range under contiguous reservation—memory that cannot become additional concurrent sequences. Paging caps internal waste at roughly one block (\(B\) tokens) per sequence (per managed cache partition) and removes most external fragmentation.

Capacity sketch
Let one token’s KV footprint (all layers, all heads, K and V) be \(b\) bytes. Contiguous reservation for \(N\) sequences costs \(\sim N L_{\max} b\). Paged on-demand costs \(\sim b\sum_i t_i\) plus \(< N B b\) partial-block slack (order-of-magnitude). The ratio \(L_{\max}/\bar{t}\) dominates the win when outputs are much shorter than the configured max.

title: PagedAttention and the KV Cache
text:
KV cache in Transformers (reminder)
For each layer \(\ell\) and head \(h\), token position \(i\) stores vectors \(k_i^{(\ell,h)}, v_i^{(\ell,h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\). Causality at decode step \(t\) uses
\[
\alpha_{t,i}=\mathrm{softmax}_i\left(\frac{q_t^\top k_i}{\sqrt{d}}\right),\qquad
o_t=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\alpha_{t,i}v_i.
\]
Prefill computes many \(q\) rows in parallel against the prompt’s \(K,V\); decode appends one new \((k_t,v_t)\) and attends with a single \(q_t\) (or a small speculative set).
Serving reality: weights are shared; KV grows per request. Throughput (tokens/s/GPU) often rises when more sequences fit—hence KV packing is a first-class systems problem, not a minor allocator tweak.

title: PagedAttention and the KV Cache
text:
Block structure
Choose block size \(B\) (vLLM commonly discusses values like 16). Logical block \(j\) holds tokens \((j-1)B+1,\ldots,jB\) (or \(0\)-based equivalents):
\[
K_j=(k_{(j-1)B+1},\ldots,k_{jB}),\qquad
V_j=(v_{(j-1)B+1},\ldots,v_{jB}).
\]
Attention becomes a loop over logical blocks: load the physical block pointed by the table, compute partial scores/outputs, advance. The last block carries a filled-token count \(1..B\).

Worked layout numbers
\(B=16\), head dim \(d=128\), dtype FP16: one head’s K block stores \(16\times 128\) elements \(=2048\) halves \(\approx 4\) KiB (order of magnitude), and V similarly. Multi-layer multi-head caches scale linearly; production engines may use separate block tables per layer/head partition or pack carefully for coalescing—design choice, not a change to the paging idea.

Allocate on demand: when decode would write past the filled count, pull a free physical block, append a table entry. Free on finish: return blocks to the pool (and decrement refcounts if shared).
decode step:

      table.append(phys)

Prefix sharing (copy-on-write intuition)
If two requests share a prompt prefix, map their early logical blocks to the same physical blocks with elevated refcounts. Divergence (different generated tokens) allocates private blocks from the fork point. Automatic prefix caching builds on the same indirection: hash logical block contents (+prefix identity) to reuse physical KV.

Custom kernels must handle variable block lists per sequence in a batch: sequence A may have 3 blocks, sequence B 40. Batching strategies (continuous batching) reshape which sequences sit in a wave while the block tables remain the source of truth for KV addresses.

Implication
A FlashAttention-style tiled softmax over a contiguous \(K,V\) buffer is not drop-in compatible. You need a kernel that:

Accepts block tables + pool base pointers, or

Materializes contiguous KV (defeats paging), or

Uses a hybrid (e.g., paged decode kernels + specialized prefill paths).

vLLM’s historical PagedAttention CUDA kernels (attention_kernels-style designs) are built for case (1): thread blocks iterate paged K/V vectors with careful vectorized loads.

title: PagedAttention and the KV Cache
text:
Paged KV layouts (kernel writer view)
Exact layouts evolve; treat the following as a mental checklist when reading kernels or writing prototypes:
Pool: physical_block[p] → storage for B tokens × head_dim (K or V)

K access for logical token t:
  j = t / B
  o = t % B
  p = block_table[seq][j]
  addr = base_K + p * stride_block + o * stride_token + head_offset

V access: similar with base_V / possibly different vectorization shape
K vs V vectorization: kernels often pack K for efficient Q·K dots (e.g., threads cooperating on a head vector) while V layouts favor weighting and accumulating into the output. Do not assume K and V share identical lane mapping.
Separate K and V caches: common—two pools, parallel tables or mirrored indices.

Illustrative host-side table (not a production kernel)
# file: toy_block_table.py
# Toy model of logical→physical mapping (host-side). Not CUDA.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

B = 16


@dataclass
class SequenceKV:
    table: list[int] = field(default_factory=list)  # physical ids
    filled: int = 0  # tokens used in last block


class BlockPool:
    def __init__(self, n_blocks: int):
        self.free = list(range(n_blocks))

    def alloc(self) -> int:
        if not self.free:
            raise MemoryError("KV pool exhausted")
        return self.free.pop()

    def free_block(self, p: int) -> None:
        self.free.append(p)


def append_token(seq: SequenceKV, pool: BlockPool) -> None:
    if not seq.table or seq.filled == B:
        seq.table.append(pool.alloc())
        seq.filled = 0
    # device would write K/V into pool[seq.table[-1]][seq.filled]
    seq.filled += 1


def release(seq: SequenceKV, pool: BlockPool) -> None:
    for p in seq.table:
        pool.free_block(p)
    seq.table.clear()
    seq.filled = 0
Use this only to reason about allocation traffic; real engines track layers/heads, CUDA streams, and fragmentation across devices.

title: PagedAttention and the KV Cache
text:
Implications for custom kernels

Indirection tax: every K/V load pays a table lookup (often cached in shared memory / registers for the active block list).

Tail blocks: masks for filled < B are mandatory—same family of bugs as ragged sequence lengths.

Batching: one wave may include many tables; prefer grouped launches or paged-friendly attention APIs over naively padding to \(L_{\max}\) contiguous.

Fusion: paging composes with continuous batching, speculative decoding (extra parallel tokens), and quantization of KV (INT8/FP8 caches)—each changes strides and scales, not the block-table story.

Swap / multi-tier: physical blocks may live in CPU RAM; kernels and schedulers must not assume all table entries are GPU-resident without a residency check.

When generating kernels with AI assistants: specify block size, K/V separation, dtype, head dim, and tail masking explicitly. Ambiguous “write attention” prompts usually emit contiguous FlashAttention clones that cannot consume a paged pool.

title: Flash-Decoding: Split-KV Attention for Long-Context Decode
text:
Flash-Decoding: Split-KV Attention for Long-Context Decode
FlashAttention made prefill fast by tiling \(QK^\top\), softmax, and \(PV\) into one kernel that never writes the score matrix to HBM. Decode is a different problem. Each step has one new query row per sequence and head, attending over a KV cache that may hold tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens. A FlashAttention-style grid parallelizes over batch × heads × query tiles, and at decode there is only one query tile. With a small batch and a long context, that leaves a handful of CTAs to stream gigabytes of KV while most SMs sit idle.
Flash-Decoding (Dao, Haziza, Massa, Sizov, 2023) adds the missing parallel dimension: the KV sequence. Each split of the cache runs the familiar online-softmax loop independently and emits a partial output plus one scalar, its log-sum-exp (LSE). A tiny second kernel then merges the splits exactly. The authors reported up to 8× faster decode for very long sequences, and the same split-then-merge pattern now sits under paged decode kernels, cascade or shared-prefix attention, and context-parallel attention across GPUs.
This chapter builds the idea from the algebra up. It proves the merge is exact, writes a two-kernel Triton implementation that you can verify on a laptop with the Triton interpreter, compiles it for a GPU you do not own, ports the production split-count heuristic, and lists the checks that catch the real bugs.

title: Flash-Decoding: Split-KV Attention for Long-Context Decode
text:
1. Why decode starves the GPU
For one (sequence, head) pair at decode step \(t\):
\[
s_i=\frac{q^\top k_i}{\sqrt d},\qquad o=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\mathrm{softmax}(s)_i\,v_i .
\]
The work is about \(4td\) FLOPs against \(2td\) elements of K and V that must be read from HBM. In FP16 that is about 1 FLOP per byte, which puts it far left on the roofline: decode attention is purely bandwidth-bound. The only goal is to keep every SM’s load pipeline full.








Kernel style
Grid at decode
CTAs for batch 1, 8 KV heads




FlashAttention (one CTA per batch × head × query tile)
\(B\cdot H\cdot 1\)
8


Flash-Decoding (adds \(S\) KV splits)
\(B\cdot H\cdot S\)
\(8S\) (e.g. 232 with \(S=29\))




Worked numbers
Batch 1, 8 KV heads (grouped-query attention), context \(128\,000\), head dim 128, FP16 cache. K plus V for one layer is
\[
2\times 8\times 128\,000\times 128\times 2\ \text{B}\approx 524\ \text{MB}.
\]
At the H100 SXM’s roughly 3.35 TB/s HBM3 peak, that is about 160 µs per layer if bandwidth is saturated. Eight CTAs on a 132-SM part cannot get close: each SM can only keep a limited number of loads in flight. Splitting the sequence 29 ways gives 232 CTAs, enough to occupy every SM and keep loads outstanding. The model is the same and so are the bytes; the kernel is simply parallelized along the dimension that actually has work.
GQA note: with grouped-query attention, several query heads share one KV head. Good decode kernels pack the query heads of a group into the “M” rows of a tile (FlashAttention-3 calls this pack_gqa), so the KV block is loaded once per group, not once per query head. The parallelism problem, and the split-KV fix, are about KV heads × batch.

title: Flash-Decoding: Split-KV Attention for Long-Context Decode
section: 2. Mental model: attention states and the merge operator
text:
2. Mental model: attention states and the merge operator
For a set of key indices \(I\), define its attention state as the pair
\[
\mathrm{LSE}(I)=\log\sum_{i\in I}e^{s_i},\qquad
o(I)=\sum_{i\in I}\frac{e^{s_i}}{e^{\mathrm{LSE}(I)}}\,v_i .
\]
\(o(I)\) is the attention output you would get if the cache contained only the keys in \(I\). \(\mathrm{LSE}(I)\) records how much total softmax mass \(I\) carries.
Claim. For disjoint \(I\) and \(J\):
\[
\mathrm{LSE}(I\cup J)=\log\!\left(e^{\mathrm{LSE}(I)}+e^{\mathrm{LSE}(J)}\right),\qquad
o(I\cup J)=\frac{e^{\mathrm{LSE}(I)}\,o(I)+e^{\mathrm{LSE}(J)}\,o(J)}{e^{\mathrm{LSE}(I)}+e^{\mathrm{LSE}(J)}} .
\]
Proof. \(e^{\mathrm{LSE}(I)}\,o(I)=\sum_{i\in I}e^{s_i}v_i\) is the unnormalized numerator over \(I\), and \(e^{\mathrm{LSE}(I)}\) is the unnormalized denominator. Numerators and denominators over disjoint sets simply add. \(\blacksquare\)
Call this merge \(\oplus\). It is associative and commutative, so the splits can be combined in any order: sequentially, as a tree, across warps, across CTAs, or across GPUs. It is the same operator FlashAttention applies tile by tile inside one CTA (the online softmax), now applied between CTAs. FlashInfer makes it the canonical output of every attention kernel (“attention state”) and exposes merge_state / merge_states as first-class operations.
Numerically stable form. Never exponentiate an LSE directly. Subtract the maximum first:
\[
m=\max_j \mathrm{LSE}_j,\qquad w_j=e^{\mathrm{LSE}_j-m},\qquad o=\frac{\sum_j w_j\,o_j}{\sum_j w_j},\qquad \mathrm{LSE}=m+\log\sum_j w_j .
\]
            KV cache for one (sequence, head):  t tokens
 ┌───────────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┬──────────┐
 │   split 0     │   split 1     │   split 2     │ split 3  │   (last split may be short or empty)
 └──────┬────────┴──────┬────────┴──────┬────────┴────┬─────┘
        │ online softmax over BLOCK_N tiles (kernel 1, one CTA per split)
        ▼               ▼               ▼             ▼
   (o0, lse0)      (o1, lse1)      (o2, lse2)    (o3, lse3)     fp32 workspace in HBM
        └───────────────┴───────┬───────┴─────────────┘
                                ▼  kernel 2: m = max lse; w = exp(lse - m); o = Σ w·o / Σ w
                         final o  (and lse, if a caller wants to merge further)

section: 3. Verify the algebra before writing a kernel
text:
3. Verify the algebra before writing a kernel
Start with a host reference so that every GPU result later has a ground truth.
# file: split_kv_reference.py
# NumPy reference: one decode query against a long KV cache, computed
#  (a) in one pass, and (b) as Flash-Decoding style splits merged by log-sum-exp.
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
D, T, S = 128, 10_000, 7            # head dim, cached tokens, number of KV splits
q = rng.standard_normal(D).astype(np.float32)
K = rng.standard_normal((T, D)).astype(np.float32)
V = rng.standard_normal((T, D)).astype(np.float32)
scale = 1.0 / np.sqrt(D)


def attend(q, K, V):
    """Return (o, lse) for one query over a KV segment: o normalised, lse = log sum exp(s)."""
    s = (K @ q) * scale
    m = s.max()
    p = np.exp(s - m)
    l = p.sum()
    return (p @ V) / l, m + np.log(l)


def merge(states):
    """Combine (o_i, lse_i) partial states into the exact full-segment state."""
    lse = np.array([st[1] for st in states])
    m = lse.max()
    w = np.exp(lse - m)                    # unnormalised weight of each split
    o = sum(wi * st[0] for wi, st in zip(w, states)) / w.sum()
    return o, m + np.log(w.sum())


o_full, lse_full = attend(q, K, V)

bounds = np.linspace(0, T, S + 1).astype(int)          # uneven split lengths are fine
parts = [attend(q, K[a:b], V[a:b]) for a, b in zip(bounds[:-1], bounds[1:])]
o_split, lse_split = merge(parts)

# The merge is associative: merging pairwise in a tree gives the same answer.
tree = merge([merge(parts[:3]), merge(parts[3:])])

print("split boundaries :", bounds.tolist())
print("max |o_full - o_split| =", float(np.abs(o_full - o_split).max()))
print("|lse_full - lse_split| =", float(abs(lse_full - lse_split)))
print("max |o_split - o_tree|  =", float(np.abs(o_split - tree[0]).max()))

pip install numpy

split boundaries : [0, 1428, 2857, 4285, 5714, 7142, 8571, 10000]
max |o_full - o_split| = 3.8762266595278316e-10
|lse_full - lse_split| = 1.7920598338605487e-10
max |o_split - o_tree|  = 1.3877787807814457e-17
Split, merge, or tree-merge: the results agree to rounding. Uneven split lengths do not matter, because each split’s LSE carries its own weight.

The trap: the textbook merge overflows
# file: merge_trap.py
# The textbook merge  o = sum(exp(lse_i) * o_i) / sum(exp(lse_i))  overflows float32
# as soon as any lse_i > ~88.7. Subtracting max(lse) first is not optional.
import numpy as np

lse = np.array([95.0, 97.5, 91.2], dtype=np.float32)        # plausible with large logits
o = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [0.5, 0.5]], dtype=np.float32)

with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    w_naive = np.exp(lse)
    print("naive weights :", w_naive)
    print("naive merge   :", (w_naive[:, None] * o).sum(0) / w_naive.sum())

m = lse.max()
w = np.exp(lse - m)
print("stable weights:", w)
print("stable merge  :", (w[:, None] * o).sum(0) / w.sum())
print("merged lse    :", m + np.log(w.sum()))
python merge_trap.py
Output:
naive weights : [inf inf inf]
naive merge   : [nan nan]
stable weights: [0.08208501 1.         0.0018363 ]
stable merge  : [0.07657673 0.92342323]
merged lse    : 97.58058
exp overflows FP32 above about 88.7, and LSE values that large are routine once logits grow (long contexts, no QK-norm, large activations). Kernels that “pass the unit test” with randn inputs and then NaN in production usually have exactly this bug in the combine step.

title: Flash-Decoding: Split-KV Attention for Long-Context Decode
text:
4. A two-kernel Triton implementation
The design is the minimum that is still honest about production concerns:

Kernel 1 (split_kv_kernel), grid \((B\cdot H,\ S)\). Each program owns one split of one (sequence, head) pair, streams its keys in BLOCK_N tiles with the online-softmax recurrence, and writes a normalized partial output and its LSE to an FP32 workspace.
Kernel 2 (combine_kernel), grid \((B\cdot H)\). Loads \(S\) LSEs and \(S\) partial outputs, applies the stable merge, and writes the result.
Ragged batches. SEQ_LENS[b] bounds every sequence, so a sequence shorter than the split layout leaves some splits empty. An empty split must write \(o=0\) and \(\mathrm{LSE}=-\infty\), giving it weight \(e^{-\infty}=0\). Writing \(0/0\) there is the classic NaN.
FP32 everywhere it matters. Scores, running max, running sum, accumulator, and workspace are all FP32, whatever the cache dtype. FlashAttention-2’s split-KV path allocates its out_accum and softmax_lse_accum workspaces in FP32 for the same reason.

# file: flash_decode_triton.py
# Two-kernel Flash-Decoding (split-KV) for batched single-token decode, written in Triton.
#   kernel 1: grid = (batch*heads, num_splits)  -> partial (o, lse) per split
#   kernel 2: grid = (batch*heads,)             -> log-sum-exp merge across splits
# Runs on a GPU, or on CPU for correctness work with:  TRITON_INTERPRET=1 python flash_decode_triton.py
import math
import os

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def split_kv_kernel(Q, K, V, SEQ_LENS, O_PART, LSE_PART,
                    stride_kb, stride_kh, stride_kt,      # K/V: [B, H, T_max, D], last dim contiguous
                    H, chunk, scale,
                    D: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr, NUM_SPLITS: tl.constexpr):
    bh = tl.program_id(0)
    split = tl.program_id(1)
    b = bh // H
    h = bh % H
    seq_len = tl.load(SEQ_LENS + b)

    start = split * chunk
    end = tl.minimum(start + chunk, seq_len)               # may be <= start: empty split

    offs_d = tl.arange(0, D)
    q = tl.load(Q + bh * D + offs_d).to(tl.float32)        # Q: [B*H, D]
    kv_base = b * stride_kb + h * stride_kh

    m_i = -float("inf")                                    # running max of scores
    l_i = 0.0                                              # running sum of exp(score - m_i)
    acc = tl.zeros([D], dtype=tl.float32)                  # running sum of p * v

    for n0 in range(start, end, BLOCK_N):
        offs_n = n0 + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N)
        mask_n = offs_n < end
        ptrs = kv_base + offs_n[:, None] * stride_kt + offs_d[None, :]
        k = tl.load(K + ptrs, mask=mask_n[:, None], other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
        s = tl.sum(k * q[None, :], axis=1) * scale         # [BLOCK_N] scores
        s = tl.where(mask_n, s, -float("inf"))
        m_new = tl.maximum(m_i, tl.max(s, axis=0))
        alpha = tl.exp(m_i - m_new)                        # rescale old state
        p = tl.exp(s - m_new)
        v = tl.load(V + ptrs, mask=mask_n[:, None], other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
        acc = acc * alpha + tl.sum(p[:, None] * v, axis=0)
        l_i = l_i * alpha + tl.sum(p, axis=0)
        m_i = m_new

    has_keys = end > start
    safe_l = tl.where(has_keys, l_i, 1.0)
    o = tl.where(has_keys, acc / safe_l, 0.0)              # empty split -> o = 0 ...
    lse = tl.where(has_keys, m_i + tl.log(safe_l), -float("inf"))  # ... with weight exp(-inf) = 0
    out = bh * NUM_SPLITS + split
    tl.store(O_PART + out * D + offs_d, o)
    tl.store(LSE_PART + out, lse)


@triton.jit
def combine_kernel(O_PART, LSE_PART, O,
                   D: tl.constexpr, NUM_SPLITS: tl.constexpr):
    bh = tl.program_id(0)
    offs_s = tl.arange(0, NUM_SPLITS)
    offs_d = tl.arange(0, D)
    lse = tl.load(LSE_PART + bh * NUM_SPLITS + offs_s)      # [S]
    m = tl.max(lse, axis=0)
    w = tl.exp(lse - m)                                     # empty splits contribute 0
    o_part = tl.load(O_PART + (bh * NUM_SPLITS + offs_s)[:, None] * D + offs_d[None, :])
    o = tl.sum(w[:, None] * o_part, axis=0) / tl.sum(w, axis=0)
    tl.store(O + bh * D + offs_d, o)


def flash_decode(q, k, v, seq_lens, num_splits=8, block_n=32):
    """q: [B, H, D]; k, v: [B, H, T_max, D]; seq_lens: [B] int32. Returns [B, H, D] float32."""
    B, H, T_max, D = k.shape
    chunk = triton.cdiv(T_max, num_splits)
    o_part = torch.empty(B * H, num_splits, D, dtype=torch.float32, device=q.device)
    lse_part = torch.empty(B * H, num_splits, dtype=torch.float32, device=q.device)
    out = torch.empty(B, H, D, dtype=torch.float32, device=q.device)
    split_kv_kernel[(B * H, num_splits)](
        q.contiguous(), k, v, seq_lens, o_part, lse_part,
        k.stride(0), k.stride(1), k.stride(2),
        H, chunk, 1.0 / math.sqrt(D),
        D=D, BLOCK_N=block_n, NUM_SPLITS=num_splits)
    combine_kernel[(B * H,)](o_part, lse_part, out, D=D, NUM_SPLITS=num_splits)
    return out


def reference(q, k, v, seq_lens):
    B, H, _, D = k.shape
    out = torch.empty(B, H, D, dtype=torch.float32)
    for b in range(B):
        L = int(seq_lens[b])
        s = torch.einsum("hd,htd->ht", q[b].float(), k[b, :, :L].float()) / math.sqrt(D)
        out[b] = torch.einsum("ht,htd->hd", torch.softmax(s, dim=-1), v[b, :, :L].float())
    return out


if __name__ == "__main__":
    device = "cpu" if os.environ.get("TRITON_INTERPRET") == "1" else "cuda"
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    B, H, T_max, D = 3, 4, 1000, 64
    seq_lens = torch.tensor([1000, 37, 1], dtype=torch.int32, device=device)  # ragged batch
    q = torch.randn(B, H, D, device=device)
    k = torch.randn(B, H, T_max, D, device=device)
    v = torch.randn(B, H, T_max, D, device=device)
    for q_gain in (1.0, 40.0):                        # 40x -> logits in the hundreds
        for splits in (1, 4, 8):
            qq = q * q_gain
            got = flash_decode(qq, k, v, seq_lens, num_splits=splits)
            ref = reference(qq.cpu(), k.cpu(), v.cpu(), seq_lens.cpu())
            err = (got.cpu() - ref).abs().max().item()
            print(f"q_gain={q_gain:>4}  num_splits={splits}:  max abs error = {err:.2e}")
Run it on a CPU with the Triton interpreter. The same file runs unchanged on a CUDA GPU without the environment variable.

text:
5. Compile for a GPU you do not have
Interpreter success does not guarantee that the kernel lowers. Loop-carried values that change dtype, non-constexpr shapes, and unsupported ops fail only in the real compiler. Triton can compile ahead of time for a named target on a CPU-only machine:
# file: compile_check.py
# Ahead-of-time compile both kernels for an H100 (sm_90) on a machine with no GPU.
# Catches type errors, bad constexpr use and loop-carried dtype mismatches before you rent a GPU.
import triton
from triton.backends.compiler import GPUTarget
from triton.compiler import ASTSource

from flash_decode_triton import combine_kernel, split_kv_kernel

target = GPUTarget("cuda", 90, 32)          # backend, compute capability, warp size
split_sig = {"Q": "*fp32", "K": "*fp32", "V": "*fp32", "SEQ_LENS": "*i32",
             "O_PART": "*fp32", "LSE_PART": "*fp32",
             "stride_kb": "i32", "stride_kh": "i32", "stride_kt": "i32",
             "H": "i32", "chunk": "i32", "scale": "fp32",
             "D": "constexpr", "BLOCK_N": "constexpr", "NUM_SPLITS": "constexpr"}
combine_sig = {"O_PART": "*fp32", "LSE_PART": "*fp32", "O": "*fp32",
               "D": "constexpr", "NUM_SPLITS": "constexpr"}

jobs = [
    ("split_kv_kernel", ASTSource(fn=split_kv_kernel, signature=split_sig,
                                  constexprs={"D": 128, "BLOCK_N": 64, "NUM_SPLITS": 32})),
    ("combine_kernel", ASTSource(fn=combine_kernel, signature=combine_sig,
                                 constexprs={"D": 128, "NUM_SPLITS": 32})),
]
for name, src in jobs:
    k = triton.compile(src, target=target)
    md = k.metadata
    print(f"{name:16s} stages={','.join(k.asm.keys())}  "
          f"num_warps={md.num_warps}  shared={md.shared} B  ptx_lines={k.asm['ptx'].count(chr(10))}")
python compile_check.py
Output (Triton 3.8.0 on a CPU-only Linux box):
split_kv_kernel  stages=source,ttir,ttgir,llir,ptx,cubin  num_warps=4  shared=128 B  ptx_lines=5067
combine_kernel   stages=source,ttir,ttgir,llir,ptx,cubin  num_warps=4  shared=0 B  ptx_lines=1035
Both kernels lower all the way to an sm_90 cubin. k.asm["ptx"] and k.asm["ttgir"] are there for inspection, and they repay it. In this build every K/V load comes out as a scalar ld.global.b32, because the hand-written signature tells the compiler nothing about pointer alignment or stride divisibility. At a normal launch, Triton specializes on arguments that are divisible by 16, and that specialization is what typically unlocks wider vector loads. Grepping the PTX of the kernel you actually launch is a cheap way to confirm you got them.
Wire this compile check, together with the interpreter test, into the agent loop as a cheap gate before any GPU time is spent.

text:
6. How many splits?
Too few splits leave SMs idle. Too many add workspace traffic and combine work, and make each split too short to amortize its prologue. FlashAttention-2’s dispatcher chooses \(S\) by wave efficiency: launch \(B\cdot H\cdot S\) CTAs onto a fixed number of slots, and prefer the smallest \(S\) whose last wave is nearly as full as the best achievable.
# file: choose_splits.py
# Wave-efficiency heuristic for picking the number of KV splits, ported from the
# FlashAttention-2 split-KV dispatcher (num_splits_heuristic in csrc/flash_attn/flash_api.cpp).
import math


def num_splits(work_items, slots, n_kv_blocks, max_splits=128):
    if work_items >= 0.8 * slots:           # already ~fills the machine: do not split
        return 1
    max_splits = min(max_splits, slots, n_kv_blocks)

    def eligible(s):                        # 11 vs 12 splits of 64 blocks is really 11 splits
        return s == 1 or math.ceil(n_kv_blocks / s) != math.ceil(n_kv_blocks / (s - 1))

    eff = {}
    for s in range(1, max_splits + 1):
        if eligible(s):
            waves = work_items * s / slots
            eff[s] = waves / math.ceil(waves)   # fraction of the last wave that is busy
    best = max(eff.values())
    return next(s for s in sorted(eff) if eff[s] >= 0.85 * best)


SMS = 132                    # e.g. H100 SXM; FA2 passes 2 * num_SMs as the slot count
BLOCK_N = 128                # KV tokens per inner tile for head_dim 128
print(f"{'batch':>5} {'heads':>8} {'context':>8} {'work':>5} {'splits':>6} {'CTAs':>5}")
for batch, heads, ctx in [(1, 8, 128_000), (1, 32, 32_000), (4, 8, 8_000),
                          (16, 8, 4_000), (64, 32, 2_000), (1, 8, 300)]:
    work = batch * heads
    s = num_splits(work, 2 * SMS, math.ceil(ctx / BLOCK_N))
    print(f"{batch:>5} {heads:>8} {ctx:>8} {work:>5} {s:>6} {work * s:>5}")

Output:
batch    heads  context  work splits  CTAs
    1        8   128000     8     29   232
    1       32    32000    32      7   224
    4        8     8000    32      7   224
   16        8     4000   128      2   256
   64       32     2000  2048      1  2048
    1        8      300     8      3    24
Reading the table:

Small batch, long context is where Flash-Decoding matters: 8 work items become 232 CTAs.
Large batch already fills the machine (2048 work items), so the heuristic returns 1 split and the extra pass is skipped entirely.
Short context is capped by the number of KV tiles: 300 tokens are only 3 tiles of 128, so at most 3 splits.
The “eligible” check skips split counts that produce the same tiles per split as a smaller count, which would add a combine for nothing.

Overhead check. Per (sequence, head), the workspace costs \(S\cdot d\) FP32 values written and read back, about \(8Sd\) bytes, while the KV stream is \(4td\) bytes in FP16. The ratio \(2S/t\) is about \(0.05\%\) for \(S=29\), \(t=128\,000\). The combine kernel should be a sliver in an Nsight Systems timeline. If it is not, \(S\) is too large or the combine is badly written.

section: 7. Where the pattern shows up in production
text:
7. Where the pattern shows up in production







System
How it uses split-KV and merge




FlashAttention-2 (≥ 2.2), flash_attn_with_kvcache
num_splits=0 selects the heuristic above; block_table= combines splits with a paged KV cache; return_softmax_lse=True returns the state for further merging


FlashAttention-3 (Hopper) interface
Exposes num_splits and pack_gqa for decode-shaped problems


FlashInfer
“Attention state” (o, lse) is the standard output; merge_state / merge_states combine segments; cascade attention computes a shared prompt prefix once for many requests and merges it with each request’s private suffix


Paged-KV decode kernels
Split boundaries are aligned to KV pages; each CTA walks its slice of the block table


Context / ring parallelism
Each GPU holds a shard of the KV sequence; the same \(\oplus\) merges partial states across devices


FlashDecoding++ (Hong et al.)
Replaces the per-split running max with a precomputed unified max to avoid synchronized rescaling, with a fallback path when values exceed it


LeanAttention
Applies Stream-K–style work partitioning to attention to reduce wave quantization



Short query blocks. Speculative decoding verifies several draft tokens at once, so \(q\) has 2–8 rows rather than 1. The same kernel shape applies, with a few query rows per CTA and the same split and merge.

section: 9. Prompting an AI assistant for a decode kernel
text:
9. Prompting an AI assistant for a decode kernel
Generated attention kernels default to prefill-shaped FlashAttention clones. State the decode contract explicitly:

Shapes: query [B, H_q, D] (or [B, q_len, H_q, D] for speculative decode), KV [B, H_kv, T_max, D] or a paged pool plus block_table, and per-sequence seq_lens.
Split-KV: the number of splits as a runtime argument, an FP32 (o, lse) workspace, and a separate combine kernel or a documented fused alternative.
Numerics: an FP32 accumulator, stable max-subtracted merge, empty split ⇒ lse = -inf and o = 0, and the LSE base stated.

Summary
Decode attention is bandwidth-bound, and at small batch the FlashAttention grid has too few CTAs to use that bandwidth. Flash-Decoding splits the KV sequence across CTAs. Each split produces an attention state \((o,\mathrm{LSE})\), and an associative, max-subtracted merge recombines the states exactly. The kernel engineering lives in the details: FP32 state, empty-split handling, ragged lengths, a split count chosen by wave efficiency, and an LSE convention stated as part of the ABI. Verify on CPU with the Triton interpreter, compile ahead of time for the target GPU, and judge the result in GB/s.

text:
DeepSeek: FlashMLA & DeepGEMM
DeepSeek stunned the AI industry by open-sourcing compact, ultra-efficient kernels that outcompeted monolithic enterprise libraries.

FlashMLA: Multi-Head Latent Attention
DeepSeek-V3 and R1 utilize Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) to compress KV caches into low-dimensional latent spaces. Standard attention kernels cannot handle this asymmetrical projection efficiently. FlashMLA is custom-tuned to decode latent vectors directly into shared memory, cutting KV memory bandwidth consumption by over 70%.


DeepGEMM: Clean Architecture over Brute Force
In fewer than 300 lines of readable, modular CUDA code, DeepGEMM implements fine-grained FP8 matrix multiplication with grouped scaling. By avoiding deeply nested template metaprogramming and focusing purely on optimal software pipelining and TMA scheduling, DeepGEMM matches and often beats commercial closed-source GEMM kernels.

Problem Track 1: Fused Sparse Attention
Implement a fused attention kernel supporting block-sparse patterns (e.g. BigBird or sliding window + global tokens). The kernel must: - Skip computation of zero-weight blocks entirely. - Maintain online softmax correctness across sparse blocks. - Outperform standard dense PyTorch attention by at least 2x on sequences >16k.


Problem Track 2: Quantized FP4/FP8 GEMM with Dynamic Dequantization
Build a high-throughput matrix multiply kernel that ingests FP8 or INT4 quantized weights and dequantizes on-the-fly inside SM registers before execution.
